name: Complementary eyeshadow for iris color

lead: This makeup approach picks eyeshadow shades that sit opposite your iris color on the color wheel, so your eyes stand out and look more vivid. Practitioners say it makes the iris pop.

It rests on color theory: contrasting hues placed near the eye are said to increase the perceived saturation of the iris through simultaneous contrast. The effect is visible the moment the shadow is on. No studies of its effect on perceived attractiveness were found.

paras: People match shadow to eye color, for example warm coppers and browns for blue eyes, or purples for green or hazel eyes, applied as normal eyeshadow in everyday or evening looks. The result shows immediately.
No specific risks beyond general cosmetic precautions such as product allergies or irritation.

angle.text: Choosing eyeshadow shades opposite your iris color on the color wheel makes the eyes look more vivid through color contrast. The effect shows as soon as the shadow is applied.

lead: Complementary eyeshadow for iris color is a makeup approach in which shadow shades are chosen from the opposite side of the color wheel to the iris, so the eyes look brighter and more vivid. Practitioners commonly pair warm copper, bronze and terracotta tones with blue eyes, plum, burgundy and bronze with green or hazel eyes, and purple, green or bronze-gold with brown eyes.[1] It is a low-cost, reversible way to make the eyes a focal point of the face without changing the eyes themselves.

Wikipedia describes eye shadow as a cosmetic applied mainly to the eyelids to make the eyes stand out, and says it can complement eye color, add depth and draw attention to the eyes. Makeup brand Jane Iredale's guide explains the principle as picking shades from the opposite side of the color wheel because contrasting hues make eyes stand out, and says shimmery or metallic finishes can echo flecks of color in the iris.[1]

Forum posts about appearance advice mention that surrounding colors can make blue eyes "pop".[2] No published trials have tested whether complementary shades change perceived attractiveness; the idea comes from color theory and makeup-artist practice.

paras: The approach starts from the iris color and selects shades that contrast with it. Jane Iredale's guide lists orange-based shades such as rich browns and terracotta for blue eyes, with gold, bronze or champagne shimmer to bring out gold flecks.[1] For green and hazel eyes, red is opposite on the wheel, and the guide suggests pinks or darker reddish tones such as bronze, rust and mahogany, and eggplant shadow, noting pure red can look less natural.[1]

For gray eyes it suggests steely shades such as silver, mink gray or icy blue. It calls brown the most versatile eye color, with deep purple, bronzy gold, mossy green or charcoal among its suggestions.[1] Shadow may be applied across the lid, on the outer corner or as a liner along the lash line, which keeps the contrast close to the iris.

Eye makeup dates to predynastic Egypt, around 5000 to 4000 BCE, where green malachite and black galena paints have been found in burials. Eye shadow became a commercial product in the 1910s in the United States, and Elizabeth Arden introduced it in her salons in 1914. It is most often sold as a powder but also comes in liquid, pencil, cream and mousse forms.

Style discussions on forums treat eye color as a feature to be highlighted with surrounding colors, including hair color and makeup.[2] Such advice is mostly given for women's makeup, though the same color logic is used in cosmetic guides generally.

lore.intro: Forum participants mention that surrounding colors can make eye color stand out.[2]
